body.statement: Let \(\ell\ge1\), let \((\eta_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\) be iid real random variables, and let \(X_i=f(\eta_i,\ldots,\eta_{i+\ell-1})\) be a square-integrable block factor. If \(S_N=\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\) and \(\sigma^2=\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(S_N)\), then \(\sigma^2=0\) if and only if there is a measurable \(g\) for which \(Y_i=g(\eta_{i+1},\ldots,\eta_{i+\ell-1})\) is square-integrable and \(X_i-\mathbb E X_i=Y_i-Y_{i-1}\) almost surely.

source.locator: Theorem 2 and the converse sentence immediately following it, Section 1
source.verbatim_statement: Let $X_k=f(\xi_k,\dots,\xi_{k+\ell-1})$ be an $\ell$-block factor for some $\ell\ge1$, where $(\xi_k)_{-\infty}^\infty$ is an \iid{} sequence. Suppose that $X_k$ has finite variance and let $\gss:=\lim_\ntoo n\qw\Var(S_n)$. If $\gss=0$, then there exists a function $g:\bbR^{\ell-1}\to\bbR$ and a constant $\mu$ such that the $(\ell-1)$-block factor $Y_k:=g(\xi_{k+1},\dots,\xi_{k+\ell-1})$ has finite variance and $X_k=Y_k-Y_{k-1}+\mu$ almost surely. The function $g$ is almost surely unique up to an additive constant. The converse is obvious in this theorem too.
